output_evals.prompt: I want to check a TOON relay's capabilities before connecting. The relay is at wss://relay.toon.example.com. How do I query its NIP-11 information?
output_evals.expected_output: Send an HTTP GET request to https://relay.toon.example.com with the header Accept: application/nostr+json. This header is critical -- without it, the relay may return HTML instead of JSON. Parse the JSON response to extract supported_nips (which NIPs the relay supports), limitation (max_message_length, max_content_length, etc.), and limitation.payment_required (true on TOON). NIP-11 tells you THAT payment is required; it does not tell you how much. For the write price, the node's ILP addresses and its settlement facts, ask the connector in front of the relay instead: GET https://proxy.relay.devnet.toonprotocol.dev/ilp returns its self-description, free and unauthenticated. A connector answers; it never announces. The relay app's own GET /health is a container healthcheck (status, pubkey, capabilities, version, timestamp) and carries no pricing. Both queries are free. NIP-11 queries are read-only HTTP requests -- no paid write needed. The relay returns standard JSON EVENT messages and speaks plain NIP-01, so no decoder is needed and any ordinary Nostr client can read it; TOON encoding applies to the sealed write payload, not to a read response.

rubric.correct: Replaces wss:// with https:// for the request URL. Includes Accept: application/nostr+json header. Explains key response fields (supported_nips, limitation, payment_required). Directs price and ILP questions to the fronting connector's GET /ilp self-description rather than to the relay. Notes no payment required for queries. States relay reads are plain NIP-01 JSON needing no decoder.
rubric.acceptable: Correctly describes the HTTP GET with Accept header and URL scheme replacement, but may not mention the self-description or all response fields.
rubric.incorrect: Omits the Accept header, uses the wss:// URL unchanged, or claims the query costs money. Claims the relay's /health or NIP-11 carries pricing, basePricePerByte, an ILP address or chain config. Claims relay reads return TOON-format strings or need a TOON decoder.

assertions: toon-write-check: Response clarifies NIP-11 is a read-only HTTP query, no paid write needed
toon-discovery-check: Response sends price questions to the connector's GET /ilp, not to the relay's /health or a kind:10032 event
toon-read-check: Response reads over plain NIP-01 and does not claim relay responses are TOON-encoded
Response includes the Accept: application/nostr+json header
Response replaces wss:// with https:// for the request URL
Response notes both NIP-11 and the self-description are free to query

output_evals.prompt: I want to publish my relay list on TOON. I use wss://relay1.toon.example.com for both reading and writing, wss://relay2.toon.example.com only for reading, and wss://relay3.toon.example.com only for writing. How do I construct and publish the kind:10002 event?
output_evals.expected_output: Construct a kind:10002 event with three r tags: ['r', 'wss://relay1.toon.example.com'] (no marker means both read and write), ['r', 'wss://relay2.toon.example.com', 'read'], and ['r', 'wss://relay3.toon.example.com', 'write']. Set content to empty string. Sign the event with your Nostr private key. Then send it: await client.send({ body: signedEvent }) from @toon-protocol/client. send() seals the payload to the terminating connector, asks that connector the route's price, mints the covering claim and carries it -- you never price the packet or sign a claim by hand. The cost is one packet: on g.toon.relay the price is flat at 1 base unit of 6-decimal USDC, so a three-relay list and a thirty-relay list cost exactly the same. kind:10002 is a replaceable event -- publishing a new one replaces the previous relay list entirely. Batch relay changes into a single update; the saving is in the number of writes, not their size. A refusal comes back as { fulfilled: false, code, message } and is never thrown; F03 means the claim did not cover the charge, and there is no F04. The relay returns standard JSON EVENT messages and speaks plain NIP-01, so no decoder is needed and any ordinary Nostr client can read it; TOON encoding applies to the sealed write payload, not to a read response.

rubric.correct: Constructs kind:10002 with correct r tags and read/write markers. Sets content to empty string. Signs the event. Sends it with client.send() from @toon-protocol/client. Treats the cost as one packet on a flat route, not as a function of size. Explains replaceable event semantics. Mentions batching updates as a way to reduce the NUMBER of writes.
rubric.acceptable: Uses client.send() with kind:10002 and correct r tag format, but may not mention replaceable semantics, batching, or the flat price.
rubric.incorrect: Calls publishEvent() or a caller-facing signBalanceProof() -- neither exists. Computes a cost by multiplying a per-byte rate by the event's size, or quotes a per-byte figure such as basePricePerByte. Reads a price from kind:10032 or a /health endpoint. Uses raw WebSocket patterns, omits read/write markers, puts content in the content field instead of tags, or uses the wrong event kind. Claims relay reads return TOON-format strings or need a TOON decoder.

assertions: toon-write-check: Response uses client.send(), not raw WebSocket and not publishEvent()
toon-fee-check: Response treats the cost as one packet on a flat route, and does NOT derive a charge from the event's byte count
toon-read-check: Response reads over plain NIP-01 and does not claim relay responses are TOON-encoded
Response includes correct r tag format with read/write markers
Response explains kind:10002 is a replaceable event
Response mentions batching relay changes to reduce the number of writes

output_evals.prompt: I want to find which relays a specific user (pubkey abc123def456) reads from and writes to. How do I discover their relay list on TOON?
output_evals.expected_output: Subscribe with filter { kinds: [10002], authors: ['abc123def456'] } to receive the user's latest relay list. Since kind:10002 is a replaceable event, you will receive at most one event. Parse the standard JSON response as on any Nostr relay. Extract the r tags from the event. Tags with no marker indicate the relay is used for both reading and writing. Tags with 'read' marker mean the user reads from that relay -- publish there if you want them to see your content. Tags with 'write' marker mean the user writes there -- subscribe there to read their events. Reading kind:10002 events is free on TOON. Note that nostr-tools SimplePool does NOT work in Node.js containers -- use direct WebSocket connections or the TOON client.

rubric.correct: Uses correct filter with kinds and authors. Explains replaceable event semantics (at most one result). Parses standard JSON. Correctly maps read/write markers to usage. Notes reading is free. Warns about SimplePool limitation.
rubric.acceptable: Uses correct filter and explains r tag semantics, but may not mention the SimplePool limitation.
rubric.incorrect: Uses wrong filter, claims multiple kind:10002 events will be returned, reverses read/write marker semantics, or claims reading costs money. Claims relay reads return TOON-format strings or need a TOON decoder.

assertions: toon-write-check: Response clarifies reading kind:10002 is read-only and free, with no paid write involved
toon-fee-check: Response notes reading kind:10002 events is free on TOON
toon-read-check: Response reads over plain NIP-01 and does not claim relay responses are TOON-encoded
social-context-check: Response explains practical meaning of read/write markers for message delivery
trigger-coverage: Eval covers kind:10002 discovery which maps to relay list triggers
Response uses correct filter with kinds: [10002] and authors array
Response correctly explains r tag read/write marker semantics

output_evals.prompt: I want to know what a TOON relay charges before I write to it, and which chain it settles on. Where does that information live?
output_evals.expected_output: Not on the relay. A TOON relay is a plain Nostr app sitting behind a connector, and the connector holds the price. Ask the connector for its self-description: GET https://proxy.relay.devnet.toonprotocol.dev/ilp, free and unauthenticated (connector ADR 0050). It carries the node's ILP addresses, its settlement facts (chain, token, decimals), the key a payload must be sealed to, and every route's price -- a base figure plus a pricePerKib when the route meters by size, longest matching prefix winning. From the client, client.describe() returns the whole document and client.routePrice(destination) returns one route's terms; null from routePrice is an answer meaning 'I do not terminate that', not a failure. A connector ANSWERS; it never announces -- there is no event that carries a node's price and no registry that collects them, and copying self-descriptions into a discovery network is a controller's job, outside the connector by definition. An unpaid request to a priced route is answered with a greeting carrying that route's terms, never the work. Live devnet, probed 2026-08-28: g.toon.relay is 1 base unit flat, g.toon.store and g.toon.relay.store are base 1000 plus 10 per KiB, g.toon.gas is 1000, all in base units of 6-decimal USDC. Settlement is USDC on Base Sepolia (evm:84532) and Solana devnet. By contrast, the relay app's own GET /health is a container healthcheck returning only status, pubkey, capabilities, version and timestamp -- no pricing, no ILP address, no chain config -- and standard NIP-11 tells you only THAT payment is required via limitation.payment_required. Both are free to query. Retired and not to be looked for: kind:10032 ILP peer info, kind:10035 SkillDescriptor, basePricePerByte, feePerByte, and a /health endpoint returning pricing.

rubric.correct: Directs the question to the connector's GET /ilp self-description, not to the relay. Names what it carries: ILP addresses, settlement facts, sealing key, and every route's price (base plus optional pricePerKib). Mentions client.describe() and/or client.routePrice(). States that a connector answers and never announces, and that kind:10032 was removed with no in-connector replacement. Correctly describes the relay's /health as liveness only. Notes both surfaces are free.
rubric.acceptable: Correctly identifies GET /ilp or client.routePrice() as the place a price comes from and distinguishes it from the relay's own endpoints, but may not list every field or mention the removed announce.
rubric.incorrect: Claims the relay's /health or NIP-11 returns pricing, an ilpAddress, peerCount, channelCount, an x402 object, TEE attestation state or a chain preset such as 'arbitrum-sepolia'. Cites basePricePerByte or feePerByte. Says a node announces itself, or invents a replacement discovery event for kind:10032. Claims querying costs money. Claims relay reads return TOON-format strings or need a TOON decoder.

assertions: toon-discovery-check: Response points at the connector's GET /ilp self-description as the source of price and settlement facts
toon-discovery-check: Response states a connector answers and never announces, and does not invent a replacement for kind:10032
toon-price-check: Response describes a price as a route schedule (base plus optional per-KiB), never as a per-byte rate
Response correctly describes the relay's own /health as liveness only, carrying no pricing
Response does NOT cite basePricePerByte, feePerByte, peerCount, channelCount, x402, TEE attestation or Arbitrum
Response notes both NIP-11 and the self-description are free to query

output_evals.prompt: How do I use NIP-66 to find online relays and check their response times? I want to build a relay selector that prioritizes low-latency relays.
output_evals.expected_output: Subscribe to kind:30166 relay discovery events with filter { kinds: [30166], #s: ['online'] } to find online relays. Each kind:30166 event is a parameterized replaceable event with a d tag set to the relay URL. Extract rtt tags for latency data: ['rtt', 'open', '<ms>'] for connection time, ['rtt', 'read', '<ms>'] for read latency, and ['rtt', 'write', '<ms>'] for write latency. Sort relays by the relevant rtt value for your use case. For TOON-specific relays, filter with #T: ['pay-to-relay']. NIP-66 data is published by third-party relay monitor services -- check kind:10166 events to find active monitors and their check frequency. NIP-66 carries no pricing. For a relay's write price, ask the connector in front of it -- GET /ilp, or client.routePrice() -- since a connector answers and never announces. All NIP-66 reading is free on TOON. The relay returns standard JSON EVENT messages and speaks plain NIP-01, so no decoder is needed and any ordinary Nostr client can read it; TOON encoding applies to the sealed write payload, not to a read response.

rubric.correct: Uses correct filter with #s for online status. Explains rtt tag structure for latency. Mentions #T filter for pay-to-relay. References kind:10166 for monitor registration. Sends price questions to the fronting connector's GET /ilp. Notes reading is free. States relay reads are plain NIP-01 JSON needing no decoder.
rubric.acceptable: Correctly describes kind:30166 subscription and rtt tags, but may not mention the pay-to-relay filter or the self-description complement.
rubric.incorrect: Uses wrong event kinds, claims NIP-66 includes ILP pricing, or describes NIP-66 as a relay-published event rather than monitor-published. Claims relay reads return TOON-format strings or need a TOON decoder.

assertions: toon-write-check: Response clarifies NIP-66 reading is read-only and free, with no paid write involved
toon-fee-check: Response notes all NIP-66 reading is free on TOON
toon-read-check: Response reads over plain NIP-01 and does not claim relay responses are TOON-encoded
social-context-check: Response notes monitor reputation trust or relay selection considerations
trigger-coverage: Eval covers kind:30166 monitoring which maps to NIP-66 relay discovery triggers
Response uses correct kind:30166 with #s filter for online status
Response explains rtt tag structure for latency measurement
Response sends price and ILP questions to the connector's GET /ilp, which NIP-66 does not carry
Response notes NIP-66 data comes from third-party monitor services

output_evals.prompt: How does TOON's payment model affect relay selection compared to free Nostr relays? What should I consider when choosing which TOON relays to list in my kind:10002?
output_evals.expected_output: On TOON, all relays require payment for writes (limitation.payment_required is true). This changes relay selection compared to free Nostr, but not along the axis you might expect. Price: each relay sits behind its own connector, and you learn its price by asking that connector -- client.routePrice(destination), or GET /ilp -- because a connector answers and never announces. There is no table to look it up in and no event that carries it. On the live relay route the price is FLAT at 1 base unit of 6-decimal USDC, so length is free and the cost lever is how OFTEN you write, not how much. Settlement compatibility: the self-description states the node's chains and tokens; settlement is USDC on Base Sepolia (evm:84532) and Solana devnet. Liveness: NIP-66 kind:30166 rtt tags for latency, plus the relay's own GET /health for a direct liveness check. Reachability: an ILP address is self-asserted -- a claim, not a grant -- so the only proof a node serves a route is that it answers for it; probe rather than assume. When choosing relays for your kind:10002 list, weigh price, settlement compatibility, latency and reachability. Publishing your relay list costs one packet regardless of how many relays it names, so batch changes into a single update rather than republishing per change -- and keep the list short for accuracy, not for cost. Send it with await client.send({ body: signedEvent }) from @toon-protocol/client. Your relay list is a public signal about which relays you trust. The relay returns standard JSON EVENT messages and speaks plain NIP-01; TOON encoding applies to the sealed write payload, not to a read response.

rubric.correct: Explains payment_required is true on all TOON relays. Obtains price by asking each fronting connector (routePrice / GET /ilp) rather than from a table or an announce. Recognises the relay route is flat, so the cost lever is the number of writes rather than their size. Covers settlement compatibility, latency and reachability. Notes a relay list update costs one packet whatever its length, and recommends batching. Discusses the relay list as a public signal.
rubric.acceptable: Correctly identifies key selection criteria and treats price as something asked of the node, but may not cover all factors or the social signal aspect.
rubric.incorrect: Claims some TOON relays are free. Compares relays by basePricePerByte or any per-byte rate. Reads a price from kind:10032, kind:10035 or a /health endpoint. Advises trimming the relay list or dropping read/write markers to save bytes. Cites TEE attestation, peerCount, channelCount, x402 or a chain preset such as 'arbitrum-sepolia'. Calls publishEvent(). Claims relay reads return TOON-format strings or need a TOON decoder.

assertions: toon-write-check: Response uses client.send() for publishing relay list updates, not publishEvent()
toon-price-check: Response compares relays by asking each connector (routePrice / GET /ilp), not by a per-byte rate
toon-fee-check: Response treats a relay list update as one packet on a flat route, not as a byte-proportional cost
Response does NOT cite basePricePerByte, TEE attestation, peerCount, channelCount, x402 or Arbitrum
Response explains the relay list is a public signal about which relays you trust
toon-read-check: Response reads over plain NIP-01 and does not claim relay responses are TOON-encoded
